name: Rukiga
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 8 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Kaji, Shigeki. 2024. Tone patterns of Rukiga nominals: An overview. Working Papers in African Linguistics 2: 29-52. Tokyo: Research Institute for Languages and Cultures of Asia and Africa (ILCAA), TUFS. Open PDF:https://tufs.repo.nii.ac.jp/records/2001374
catalog_locator: Section 2 'Tone value' and 2.2 'H tone as F tone', pp. 30-31 (fn. 3 p. 30, fn. 5 p. 31); Section 5.1.1 'High tone anticipation', pp. 35-36
catalog_quote: Rukiga has two basic tones, high (H) and low (L). H is indicated with an acute accent mark over the vowel (á), and L is unmarked. Falling tone (F), marked with a circumflex over the vowel (â), appears. Rising tone (R) does not appear. [...] H tone does not appear every time as H. Characteristically, it becomes F in penultimate heavy syllables in utterance-final position, as in (3). [...] Notably, F tone appears only on the heavy penultimate syllable of words. It never appears on the antepenultimate or more left syllable of words, even though the syllable has a long vowel. It does not appear on the final syllable of words either because the final syllable of words does not accommodate two moras in Rukiga. [fn. 3, p. 30] We do not consider the theoretical question of whether the opposition is either H vs. L or H vs. Ø. Simply, H and L are used. In this paper, the term “tone” is used both phonologically (as opposed to accent) and phonetically. [p. 36] Notably, in the examples in (15), the H tone of the last and penultimate syllables of words is anticipated. [...] The HTA of the penultimate syllable of words is characteristic of Rukiga tone. In other languages in the area, including Runyankore, HTA occurs only of H tone of the last syllable of words
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress
sweep_summary: Chiga (chig1238) is not in the catalog. All three title-keyword items are print-only: (1) Philippson 1991/92 thesis (Paris 5, 542 pp; Glottolog links it to Chiga among ~50 East African Bantu languoids) - only the theses.fr abstract is online, which frames the survey as running from purely tonal systems to purely demarcative penultimate stress, with the emergence of penultimate accent as the hypothesised driver of change; the Chiga-specific classification was not seen; priority medium. (2) Johnson 1976 'Devoicing, tone and stress in Runyankore' (SCOPIL 3, pp. 207-216) - HathiTrust search-only, no Google Books preview; describes Runyankore (nyan1307), the sister variety in the Nkore-Kiga cluster; the most likely explicit statement on stress for this cluster; priority high. (3) Ohly 1982 (Kiswahili 49: 93-97) on stress assimilation of Swahili/Oriental loanwords in Runyankore - HathiTrust search-only, AJOL only from vol. 70; secondary loanword evidence; priority medium. No first-hand word-stress statement for Chiga was read in this search of works with stress in the title (no new stress statement was found); the open Rukiga/Runyankore literature already held by the project (Kaji, Yukawa, Hyman, Poletto, Van der Wal & Asiimwe, Asiimwe) describes a H/L tone system with utterance-final penultimate falling tone on heavy syllables and no word-final phonetic lengthening (Kaji 2024), but says nothing about stress placement. StressTyp2 has no Nkore-Kiga entry.fr, HAL, HathiTrust bib API, Open Library, archive.org, Crossref, Glottolog and StressTyp2 directly.

Falling tone (F), marked with a circumflex over the vowel (â), appears. Rising tone (R) does not appear." Section 2.2 (p. 31, lines 101-102): "H tone does not appear every time as H. Characteristically, it becomes F in penultimate heavy syllables in utterance-final position, as in (3)." Lines 115-117: "Notably, F tone appears only on the heavy penultimate syllable of words. It never appears on the antepenultimate or more left syllable of words, even though the syllable has a long vowel."…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Rukiga is described as a two-tone (H/L) language with lexically placed H; no word stress is described. Prosodic prominence effects are tonal and positional: a lexical H on a heavy penultimate syllable is realised as falling before pause, and the H of a word-final or penultimate syllable is anticipated (shifted leftward) in isolation. The sister variety Runyankore (Hyman 2020, p. 53) is likewise a privative /H/ vs Ø system in which a prepausal final H is retracted onto the penult.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Kaji notes northern vs southern Rukiga dialect differences in tone (Section 6) and that Runyankore lacks the two-H nominals and penultimate-H anticipation of Rukiga; Yukawa 2002 (p. 2) reports Taylor's 'Low Speakers' vs 'High Speakers' distinction in Kiga/Nkore tone.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone patterns given for nouns in isolation; the F-tone realisation and the anticipation rule are stated for utterance-final (prepausal) position, i.e. phrase-level conditioning on word tone. No source opened uses the word 'stress' for Rukiga or Runyankore.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source (Kaji 2024) describes Rukiga proper, mainly the southern dialect around Lake Bunyonyi (Kabale), i.e. Chiga chig1238; Kaji notes tonal differences between northern and southern Rukiga and between Rukiga and Runyankore. The Hyman 2020/2023 and Poletto 1996/1998 items describe Runyankore (Nyankore, Glottolog nyan1307), the closely related variety usually grouped with Rukiga as 'Runyankore-Rukiga' (Taylor's 'Nkore-Kiga'); Yukawa 2002 describes Kiga from a Kabale-raised speaker. Van der Wal & Asiimwe 2020 and Asiimwe 2024 are Rukiga (JE14).

new_statements.translation: In group III, Nyoro, Tooro and a certain number of Nyankore and Kiga sub-dialects have lost every distinctive prosodic system and replaced it with a system of demarcative accent on the penultimate. / Tableau II: '(a) 3 tonal patterns for disyllabic nominal stems, (b) 2 for verbo-nominals': most Nyankore-Kiga sub-dialects, Haya; versus '(a) 1, (b) 1, (c) no grammatical use of prosody': Nyoro/Tooro, some Nyankore/Kiga sub-dialects. / §3.5.2 b) languages with a pitch peak, but no length peak, on the penultimate (languages without distinctive prosodemes but with a length contrast): Nyoro, Tooro, some Nyankore and Kiga sub-dialects. / Annexe, Nyankore (other dialects): accentual language with H melody; 3 patterns -cv(:)cv, -c*v(:)cv, -cv(:)c*v; H associates to the accented syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's 'tonal' record (Kaji 2024: H vs L, falling tone only on a heavy penult utterance-finally). Philippson analyses the majority Nyankore-Kiga system as accentual with an H melody (three lexical accent patterns on disyllabic noun stems, H on the accented syllable), i.e. a restricted tone / pitch accent framing of the same lexical pitch contrasts, and adds two penult statements: a final H retracts to the penultimate before pause (cf. Kaji's utterance-final F on the penult), and some Nyankore and Kiga sub-dialects have lost distinctive tone altogether and carry a demarcative penultimate pitch accent. Kaji's Rukiga (lexical H/L contrasts) evidently belongs to Philippso…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Philippson splits Nyankore-Kiga (his group III, Rutara) in two. (1) Most Nyankore-Kiga sub-dialects (data second-hand: Johnson 1976, Taylor 1959, Morris 1964; he states the Nyankore system is identical to Haya's 'à quelques infimes détails près') are 'accentual languages with an H melody': disyllabic nominal stems carry one of three lexically given patterns (unaccented -cvcv, accent on stem-initial -c*vcv, accent on final -cvc*v), the H tone associates to the accented syllable, Meeussen's rule applies, a final mark dissimilates preceding ones, and post-lexically a final H is retracted onto the penultimate before pause (in some speakers -cvc*v is realised -cvcv, in others -c*vcv, before pause). This is a restricted-tone / pitch accent analysis of the same H-vs-L facts the catalog records as tonal. (2) 'A certain number' of Nyankore and Kiga sub-dialects, like Nyoro and Tooro, have lost all distinctive tone and have instead a demarcative accent = pitch culmination on the penultimate syllable (no penultimate lengthening; vowel length remains contrastive). He does not identify which Kiga sub-dialects belong to (2).
new_statements.exceptions: Dialect split: unnamed Nyankore/Kiga sub-dialects with no lexical tone and fixed penultimate demarcative pitch accent (grouped with Nyoro/Tooro); in Kerebe and some Nyankore/Kiga sub-dialects the final-accent pattern -cvc*v has merged into toneless -cvcv (p.188); one lexical exception noted for the Rutara HH>HB reduction ('nez' omwo:Ng*o, fn. p.412). Kiga itself has no section of its own: every Kiga statement is made jointly with Nyankore.
new_statements.identity_note: Philippson 1991 has no Kiga-specific section: Kiga (Guthrie E14) is listed in his group III (Rutara) beside Nyankore (E13) and every prosodic statement about it is made jointly as 'nyankore/kiga' or 'nyankore et kiga', with the detailed annexe summary given under 'Nyankore (autres dialectes)' and the toneless penult-accent type under 'Nyoro/Tooro (certains dialectes = nyoro/tooro)'. His Nyankore sources are Johnson 1976 (Runyankore), Taylor 1959 (Runyankore-Rukiga dictionary with tone marks) and Morris 1964 (Bahima of Ankole). The catalog record (Kaji 2024) describes Rukiga proper as spoken by Kaji's Kabale-area consultants.

sources.quote: This work studies the very diverse prosodic systems of east African bantu languages, on the basis of non-linear (autosegmental and metrical) phonology. We find a one end purely tonal systems (like kikuyu) and at the other end systems with purely demarcative penultimate stress, with all intermediate cases. [...] a hypothesis is presented according to which the emergence of penultimate accent is the main cause of the evolution of these systems.
sources.note: Comparative tone/accent survey of ~50 East African Bantu languages including Chiga (Glottolog ref 38907); likely to classify Nkore-Kiga as tonal vs accentual and to note any penultimate prominence. theses.fr 1992PA05H011 records it as not accessible online.

sources.note: 'Accent' = tone: acute for H, circumflex for falling, unmarked L (existence of falling doubtful).
